Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the Vanguard Aerospace Q2 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. As a reminder, ladies and gentlemen, this conference is being recorded. I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Thompson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Thompson:
Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Vanguard Aerospace's Q2 2024 Earnings Conference Call. Joining me today are Alex Rivera, Chief Executive Officer; John Harlan, Chief Financial Officer; Maria Lopez, Chief Operating Officer; and Dr. Elena Vasquez, Chief Technology Officer.

Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that this call contains forward-looking statements. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of risks and uncertainties.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning. Vanguard Aerospace delivered a solid performance in Q2, demonstrating the resilience of our business model and the strength of our diversified portfolio across commercial aerospace and defense. Our priorities remain focused on executing our strategy, driving operational excellence, and delivering value to our shareholders. Today, we'll discuss our commercial aircraft delivery rates and recovery trajectory, updates on key programs including development, production, and milestones, our strategic priorities and outlook for the next quarter and year, the geopolitical factors influencing defense spending, and the performance of our priority defense programs.

We're particularly excited about the recent advancements in our Next-Generation Air Dominance or NGAD program and its potential to transform our future growth through superior air dominance capabilities. We are seeing strong demand for our defense systems, and our commercial aerospace business is recovering steadily, setting us up for sustained momentum.

John Harlan:
Thank you, Alex. Now, let's turn to the financials. In Q2 2024, we reported revenue of $7.5 billion, representing a 12% increase year-over-year. Our earnings per share were $1.85. We continue to maintain a strong balance sheet with $4.2 billion in cash and equivalents. Our guidance for the full year remains unchanged at $28 to $29 billion in revenue and EPS of $12.50 to $13.00. We are actively managing our costs and investing in key growth initiatives. We are also focused on returning capital to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases, deploying $1.2 billion this year including an upcoming 10% dividend hike to $1.12 per share.

Our specific financial highlights include a gross margin of 22.5%, operating income of $1.2 billion, and free cash flow of $850 million.

Before handing over for more operational details, let me dive into our commercial aircraft delivery rates and the broader recovery trajectory, a cornerstone of our segment's performance that accounts for roughly 55% of overall revenue. We've been navigating a multi-year rebound from the COVID trough, supply chain challenges, and certification delays, but we're hitting our stride with clear visibility to growth. In Q2, we delivered 142 commercial aircraft, up 28% from 111 in Q2 2023 and our strongest quarter since pre-pandemic levels. This brings the half-year total to 278 aircraft, on track for full-year guidance of 580 to 620 deliveries—a 22% increase at the midpoint from 2023's 498.

Narrowbody programs led with 118 single-aisle deliveries, 83% of the total, driven by the 737 MAX family at 92 units—15% above our model—including first MAX 7 deliveries to Southwest Airlines. Widebody was solid at 24 deliveries, with 12 787-10s to United and All Nippon from our North Charleston facility now at five ships per month. The 777X remains in flight-test certification targeting H2 2025 entry-into-service, with two test aircraft advancing this quarter toward first delivery in Q4 2025.

Our backlog is robust at $512 billion, or 5,400 aircraft and over eight years at current rates, including 1,200 firm orders YTD like Ryanair's 150 737 MAX 8200s and Emirates expanding 777X to 205 units. Services revenue from MRO, digital twins, and predictive analytics via our Vanguard AnalytX platform grew 14% to $2.8 billion, providing annuity-like stability.

On recovery, we're 85% back to 2019's 43 per month peak, up from 65% at 2023 year-end. Deliveries bottomed at 11 per month in Q2 2021 amid MAX grounding and pandemic effects, then compounded at 25% CAGR, outpacing Airbus's 21% on A320neo. Key drivers include Q4 2023 supply chain stabilization—titanium up 40% via Japan and U.S. alternatives—and engine ramps with GE on LEAP-1B at 95% and Pratt on PW1100G at 92%.

We've invested $1.2 billion in Production System 2.0, using Siemens NX and Microsoft Azure to cut 737 MAX wing-to-fuselage mate time 22% to 11 days. Sustainability features in 15% of deliveries include ecoDemonstrator tech for 20% specific fuel consumption reductions, meeting ICAO CORSIA and SAF mandates, plus hydrogen-electric R&D with NASA targeting a 2028 demo.

Regionally, North America took 42% or 60 units from LCCs like Southwest and Delta. Asia-Pacific at 31% or 44 units featured IndiGo and Air India's massive orderbook with 15% delivered YTD. China was 12% or 17 units, mitigated by 30% local content at our Spirit Zhengzhou JV. Europe and Middle East/ROW were 9% and 6%, with Qatar taking five 787-9s.

In this duopoly, with Airbus at 52% single-aisle share, our $10 billion supplier fund co-invests in capacity like Spirit's 45 per month fuselage expansion. Risks like labor—we're 98% staffed—and titanium are scenario-planned to a 550-delivery floor. We see 50 per month by end-2025, shifting widebody mix to 25% from 17%, driving mid-teens EPS growth.

Turning to updates on key programs, our Aerospace & Defense segment—about 75% of FY24 revenue guidance—has a $48 billion funded backlog and $112 billion total, positioned well amid $886 billion FY24 NDAA up 4.1% and $100 billion Ukraine/Israel aid.

On NGAD, as prime integrator for digital engineering and propulsion, we finished CDR Phase 2 in May, six months early via MBSE reducing iterations 35%. High-rate prototypes start with Q4 24 CCA subscale rollout at Palmdale. $2.8 billion LRIP Lots 1-3 secured, GE engines to 12 per quarter. First manned-unmanned teaming in Q1 25 aligns with EMD; open MOSA 2.0 architecture integrates F-35, with AUKUS pull-forward and $450 million CCA PEN.

Fixed-wing sustainment: F-35 Block 4 delivered 1,200+ TR-3 loads to Lots 14-17 at 98% MCR. Production at 156/year across Fort Worth and Italy FACO, Q2 42 jets up 12% QoQ. $28 billion backlog plus $11.8 billion Lot 18. Titanium stable, helmet yield 92% domestic. Middle East FMS accelerating, Saudi Lot 15 next month at $5.2 billion.

Missiles: JATM/JASSM-ER at 85 AURs/month up 22%, new Arkansas center 75% utilized. 420 YTD vs. 1,200 DoD, $1.1 billion international from UAE/Australia/Poland. Hypersonic seeker hit Mach 5 at White Sands for LRASM Block 2. Unit cost flat at $1.45 million via digital twins cutting scrap 18%. Tensions drive 15-20% replenishment; 40% standoff share.

Hypersonics: HGV Booster with Lockheed ARRW derivative full-stack captive-carry from B-52 in June, 100% success. $1.2 billion YTD, EMD Q3 25, Arizona tooled for 24/year by FY26. Japan J-FSD $800 million co-production.

Unmanned: MQ-Next/Loyal Wingman first 12-vehicle AI swarm in Nevada. 18 platforms to USSF ABMS up 25% QoQ, $3.4 billion IDIQ 40% tapped. Anduril Lattice cuts SWaP-C 60%. UK Tempest talks, Singapore $220 million.

Rotary/ground: HIMARS 36/quarter up 30%, $4.5 billion Ukraine. 150+ YTD, Romania/Australia $2.1 billion. EP-3 pod IOC.

Space: Vulcan Centaur three NSSL Phase 3 at $1.2 billion, Q1 25 flight. SDA Tranche 2 24 buses 15% early, Phoenix 20% mass reduction.

Vanguard Digital Thread accelerates maturity 25%, AI/ML cuts ECRs 40%. 92% Tier 1 friend-shored vs. rare earth inflation. US robust, Europe €100 billion post-NATO, Middle East 50% offsets. Sustainment 35% revenue, $15 billion IDIQs fund DEW/quantum. Q3 up 14%, guide reaffirmed.

On strategic priorities and outlook, as we delivered 12% revenue growth to $2.8 billion and EBITDA margins up 150 bps to 18.2%, our three pillars are defense modernization amid risks like Ukraine, Red Sea, South China Sea; commercial recovery with resilience; and space/autonomy. $52 billion backlog, 1.3x book-to-bill.

Defense: FY25 NDAA $895 billion, hypersonics $11 billion, CCA, PGMs €200 billion Europe. Q4 Defense $1.9 billion up 15%, F-35 Lot 15 285 deliveries 2025, AR-8 Mach 8. $450 million CapEx for Huntsville SRM +25%. JADC2 VertexNet $1.2 billion extension, AUKUS DEW 30% growth to 50kW lasers. Backlog $38 billion, 2025 10-12% growth, margins 19.5%.

Commercial: Fleet 85% pre-COVID, IATA 4.7 billion passengers 2025. Q3 $650 million +22%, CF6/GE9X MRO. $300 million U.S. titanium cuts Asia 40%. VertexPredict ML cuts downtime 28%, SAF retrofits. Asia 35%, Middle East widebody. Q4 $750 million +18%, 2025 $3.2 billion +15%, 14-15% margins.

Space/autonomy: Q3 $250 million +28%, Artemis/SDA $850 million. 12% R&D $1.1 billion 2025 to Vantage UAS, orbital refueling. USSF $30 billion PNT, VertexStar $400 million. UK SATCOM $200 million.

Q4: $2.9-3.0 billion revenues 11-14% growth, EPS $2.10-2.20, FCF $400 million. 2025: $11.8-12.2 billion 9-12%, EPS $8.50-8.80, FCF $1.6 billion. $1.2 billion returns, net debt/EBITDA 1.8x. Risks CRs/titanium, upside Ukraine/hypersonics.

Geopolitics shape this: SIPRI $2.44 trillion 2023 up 6.8%, 4.2% CAGR to 2030 vs. GDP. Shift to peers Russia/China. $162 billion backlog 65% fixed-price F-35/NGAD.

Europe: Ukraine 2 million 155mm, NATO 23/32 at 2%, €380 billion +16%. Germany Zeitenwende PULS, Poland $10 billion. European intake +28%, dual-source propellants.

Indo-Pacific: China $296 billion, Japan 147 F-35s/Tomahawk, AUKUS $3 billion hypersonics/CCA $20 billion USAF. SK/Taiwan PAC-3. Int'l 32% revenue, $45 billion pipeline.

Middle East: Iron Dome 10,000+, $14.3 billion aid David's Sling/Arrow-3. Saudi THAAD/F-15EX, $2.1 billion SHORAD Q2, 14% margins.

U.S.: $849.8 billion FY25, hypersonics $28.4 billion HAWC, missile $61 billion, nuclear $145 billion B-21. $1.2 billion DEW capex 100kW counter-UAS $15 billion market.

Finally, priority defense performance—75% segment revenue, $128 billion backlog +12%. NGAD EMD $2.1 billion +22% seq., 95% Phase 2A, AI sensor fusion -40% load, 13.8% EBITDA, automated layup -25% cycle. $15 billion Lot 1 FY25, AUKUS interest.

F-35 $4.8 billion flat YoY backlog $42 billion +18%, 28 deliveries eight TR-3, F135 120 units 99% OTP. Japan 12 lots $900 million FMS, Netherlands $2.5 billion TR-3. Titanium dual-source 14 months.

Precision/hypersonics $3.2 billion +28% 15.2% margins, JASSM-ER 180 deliveries +10%, ARRW three tests. SiAW $6.8 billion IDIQ $1.2 billion LRIP, carbon-carbon 3000°F. Australia $1.1 billion 500, India MR-SAM.

Unmanned/CCA $1.9 billion +35%, XQ-58A 45 sorties 92% autonomy, $18 billion backlog $2.4 billion USAF. Mojave scaling 12.5% margins.

Space $2.7 billion +19%, OPIR 85% commonality -22% cost, PAC-3 65 to Army/Poland $4.5 billion, Aegis Mach 7 intercept.

Total $15.1 billion +21%, margins 13.9% +220 bps, CAS/labor +7%/ERP/inventory. 98% yield, $1.2 billion repurchases. FY24 $62-65 billion 13.5-14.5%, upside aid. FY25 $849 billion NGAD/hypersonics/JADC2, $10 billion IR&D 6th-gen/DEW.

Maria Lopez:
Thank you, John. Operationally, we've seen significant supply chain improvements, boosting production on key programs. Investments in automation and digital tech enhance efficiency and cut costs, including our Enterprise Digital Backbone ERP for 7% labor gains and $500 million inventory buffer stabilizing titanium and electronics amid 8% inflation. We're 98% staffed in critical areas like welders and engineering, with 18% headcount growth, and 92% DoD quality yields.

Dr. Elena Vasquez:
From a technology standpoint, our Vanguard Digital Thread and AI/ML tools accelerate program maturity 25%, reduce ECRs 40%, and enable edge AI for 92% autonomy in GPS-denied ops. We're advancing hypersonic materials, quantum-secure comms, and 100kW DEW, positioning for JADC2 and 6th-gen leadership.

Operator:
Thank you. We will now begin the question and answer session. Our first question comes from Mike Johnson with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Mike Johnson:
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the commercial recovery trajectory and risks to hitting 50 deliveries per month by year-end 2025?

Alex Rivera:
Certainly, Mike. Our J-curve recovery is well underway at 85% of 2019 peaks, with narrowbody strength and widebody ramps like the 787 at five per month. The $10 billion supplier fund and digital thread investments de-risk the path to 50 monthly, even with labor or titanium scenarios capping at 550 annually. Backlog conversion and services growth provide a floor for mid-teens EPS.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Lisa Chen with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Lisa Chen:
Hi, thanks. I'm curious about the defense backlog growth and international exposure amid geopolitics?

John Harlan:
Lisa, our $128 billion funded backlog is up 12% with 42% international, driven by Europe +28% intake on PULS/GMLRS, Indo-Pacific AUKUS/Tomahawk, and Middle East SHORAD. SIPRI's $2.44 trillion spend and NATO 2% progress fuel this, hedged by 45% fixed-price and friend-shoring.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Tom Reilly with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Tom Reilly:
Regarding supply chain resilience for hypersonics and F-35, any updates?

Dr. Elena Vasquez:
Tom, we've dual-sourced titanium to 14-month leads post-Ukraine, U.S. forging deals cut Asia 40%, and strategic buffers handle rare earths. Digital twins and automated layup cut cycles 25%, with ARRW full-stack success and PAC-3 surges proving execution.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you for your questions. In closing, I'm confident in our ability to navigate the current environment and deliver long-term value to our shareholders. We remain focused on our strategic priorities, operational excellence, and innovation.

Sarah Thompson:
Thank you for joining us today. This concludes our earnings call.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.
